name: Igor In the Museum
description: Igor is in the museum and he wants to see as many pictures as possible. Museum can be represented as a rectangular field of n × m cells. Each cell is either empty or impassable. Empty cells are marked with ' . ', impassable cells are marked with ' * '. Every two adjacent cells of different types (one empty and one impassable) are divided by a wall containing one picture. At the beginning Igor is in some empty cell. At every moment he can move to any empty cell that share a side with the current one. For several starting positions you should calculate the maximum number of pictures that Igor can see. Igor is able to see the picture only if he is in the cell adjacent to the wall with this picture. Igor have a lot of time, so he will examine every picture he can see.
input_specification: First line of the input contains three integers n , m and k ( 3 ≤ n , m ≤ 1000, 1 ≤ k ≤ min ( n · m , 100 000) ) — the museum dimensions and the number of starting positions to process. Each of the next n lines contains m symbols ' . ', ' * ' — the description of the museum. It is guaranteed that all border cells are impassable, so Igor can't go out from the museum. Each of the last k lines contains two integers x and y ( 1 ≤ x ≤ n , 1 ≤ y ≤ m ) — the row and the column of one of Igor's starting positions respectively. Rows are numbered from top to bottom, columns — from left to right. It is guaranteed that all starting positions are empty cells.
output_specification: Print k integers — the maximum number of pictures, that Igor can see if he starts in corresponding position.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 598D — Igor In the Museum [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
